NVIDIA has launched a family of compact desktop PCs built around its local AI strategy, now available from ASUS, Dell, and MSI. These systems bring local AI agents, image and video generation, and model fine-tuning to a dedicated Windows PC. The RTX Spark compact desktops offer up to 128GB of unified memory alongside NVIDIA's AI software stack, providing room for larger local models plus RTX-accelerated creative and development tools. A dedicated desktop can keep agents and scheduled tasks running while a laptop travels or handles other work.

The hardware is equipped with a 20-core NVIDIA Grace CPU, an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU with 6,144 CUDA cores, up to 128GB of unified memory, delivering up to 1 petaflop of AI performance. Ten-gigabit Ethernet connectivity enables fast transfers of large datasets, model files, and creative assets between the desktops and networked storage. This configuration allows running massive 120-billion-parameter large language models locally, rendering 90GB+ 3D scenes in real time, and smoothly editing 4:2:2 video in real time.

Running supported models locally keeps data on-device and avoids per-token cloud API charges for those tasks. Alongside the new desktops, an expanding software ecosystem brings more creative and development workflows to RTX Spark laptops and compact desktops. Native Windows on Arm applications from Adobe, the NVIDIA DLSS Ray Reconstruction feature in Blender, and local generation workflows in ComfyUI expand what creators and developers can do — all on one Windows PC.

For developers, native CUDA support and Linux development tools through Windows Subsystem for Linux provide a foundation for building and running local AI workflows. Developers can set up agents with Hermes Agent or NVIDIA NemoClaw blueprints and fine-tune supported models using Unsloth. RTX Spark can run creative agents that connect familiar applications and local AI tools, helping creators move from an idea to finished work with natural-language instructions.

NVIDIA Switchyard, now available in Hermes, automatically routes agent tasks between local and cloud models — everyday tasks run on device while advanced reasoning draws on cloud models, helping manage cloud costs. These capabilities come together in creative workflows connecting Photoshop and ComfyUI through Hermes Agent, where creators can turn sketches into rendered images and animations or animate an image entirely on device.

Adobe is expanding native Windows on Arm support and RTX acceleration across its creative applications. Adobe Premiere accelerates AI-powered editing features including Enhance Speech, Object Mask, Scene Edit Detection, and Auto Reframe through NVIDIA TensorRT-RTX. The update improves professional video format support — Canon RAW, Red RAW, ARRI RAW, ARRICORE, ARRI HDE, H.264, HEVC in MXF, ProRes RAW, and long-GOP video — letting editors realize more than 50% quicker turnaround on everyday H.264 video deliverables.

Adobe Photoshop adds TensorRT-RTX acceleration for the Remove Tool and ArmRTX Spark-native Camera Raw support. Adobe Substance 3D Painter 12.2 is now optimized for RTX Spark with native Arm support in public beta, requiring no compatibility layer. Adobe Illustrator and InDesign now offer native Windows on Arm versions; Illustrator delivers up to 30% higher performance than its emulated version.

Blender 5.3 integrates DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction into the Cycles viewport, delivering near-final-quality lighting, reflections, and materials in real time — requiring Blender 5.3 and the latest NVIDIA Game Ready Driver or Studio Driver.

Separately at Microsoft Ignite, Windows Server is evolving for organizations running AI closer to enterprise applications and data. The NVIDIA DGX Station for Windows platform powered by the GB300 Grace Blackwell Ultra Desktop Superchip now supports Windows Server 2028. Developers can bring any GGUF model from Hugging Face into Windows ML using the llama.cpp backend, or use the experimental DxCGC backend to compile and run models through DirectX 12 alongside graphics.

In related local AI updates, llama.cpp v1.0.0 introduces API versioning with expanded model support and CUDA optimizations for NVFP4 inference. Ricursive Intelligence introduced Ripple-65B Preview, trained on NVIDIA B300 GPUs and refined using Nemotron post-training datasets, running locally on DGX Spark. Runway's Praxis-1 is a 27-billion-parameter world action model that predicts video and actions together, runnable on the RTX 5090, RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, DGX Spark, and DGX Station with LoRA fine-tuning support.

Still coming soon are mini PCs from Acer, GIGABYTE, and HP, along with the Microsoft Surface RTX Spark Dev Box. The NVIDIA Local AI newsletter is available for updates.
items.title: NVIDIA RTX Spark Compact Desktops Launch with Local AI Capabilities and Expanded Software Support

items.summary: Training next-generation machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) requires tens to hundreds of millions of density functional theory (DFT) calculations for energies, forces, and stresses across diverse structures and chemistries. VASP is the dominant plane-wave DFT implementation used at national labs and research institutions as a gold standard for generating this data. As MLIP datasets grow, pressure mounts to generate DFT data faster and cheaper; however, small unit cells and dense k-point grids common in MLIP generation can leave GPU performance unused. While VASP's OpenACC implementation has delivered meaningful speedups especially for large systems, sequential k-point processing limits utilization on smaller systems, and AI workloads are reshaping GPUs toward lower-precision data types, widening the gap between modern NVIDIA hardware and FP64-only HPC codes.
items.title: Tackling GPU Bottlenecks in Plane-Wave DFT with K-Point Batching and Mixed Precision

In five years Anthropic has grown from an unknown start-up into a tech giant valued at more than a trillion dollars. The company, behind the AI platform Claude, is floating on the US stock exchange and plans to sell shares between $70 and $78 each. At the highest price of $78, founders' shareholdings would be worth at least $18.5bn each.

The firm was formed by seven people who left rival OpenAI in 2021. Dario Amodei, now 43, is chief executive and the person his sister says makes the company 'ambitious'. In 2020 he worked at OpenAI when it launched Chat-GPT before leaving to found Anthropic with his sister Daniela and five colleagues. He grew up in San Francisco, studied physics at Princeton and Stanford, then switched to biology and biomedical sciences after his father died from hepatitis C. Before joining OpenAI he did stints at Baidu and Google; he left because some people within the company were putting profit before safety.

Daniela Amodei is 39 and president of Anthropic, managing the executive team while leading research, engineering, product, governance and commercial work. She studied English Literature at UC Santa Cruz, worked for Democrat representative Matt Cartwright, and was head of risk operations at Stripe. She followed her brother into OpenAI when he left.

Tom Brown is 39 and chief compute officer, responsible for how Anthropic secures and uses computing resources. He led GPT-3 engineering at OpenAI after working on Google's DeepMind project, and earlier co-founded an app called 'Grouper'. He has supported Donald Trump's stance on datacentres.

Jack Clark is 37 and head of public benefit; he also leads the Anthropic Institute think tank. Originally from Brighton in the UK, he studied English Literature and Creative Writing at the University of East Anglia before becoming a technology journalist for ZDNet UK, The Register, and Bloomberg, then joining OpenAI.

Jared Kaplan is 42 and chief science officer heading technical research; he is also an associate professor at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore. He holds a PhD in physics from Harvard University, and his work on scaling laws has helped AI firms predict model behaviour.

Chris Olah is interpretability research lead, focused on how AI models work with each other. The New York Times describes him as 'boyish' but with 'the zeal of an evangelist', reporting that he spent much of the last year meeting faith leaders to explore morality and AI. He previously led interoperability research at OpenAI and was a Google Brain research scientist, earning a $100,000 Thiel Fellowship after leaving Toronto University early.

Sam McCandlish is 36 and chief architect, helping shape policy to mitigate AI risks; he worked on safety at OpenAI before. He will own around 1.6% of the company once shares are sold. He has a physics PhD from Stanford and maths and physics degrees from Brandeis University outside Boston.
items.title: Anthropic Founders Set to Become Multi-Billionaires on IPO

items.summary: A petition signed by roughly 197,000 people, including Elon Musk, called on Nvidia to reinstate ousted CEO Jensen Huang. The article frames one reason behind the campaign as that Huang had used Nvidia's profits to help finance the AI boom he championed. Nvidia reported net income of $64.9 billion for its third quarter, up from $59.7 billion in the prior quarter. Under Huang, the company aggressively invested in AI startups and neoclouds and began guaranteeing large loans to finance new data centers. Its largest deal was a $105 billion backstop for OpenAI's PORTS-Pike campus in Ohio, announced in August; in exchange, OpenAI promised exclusive use of Nvidia equipment. Huang's departure raised questions about whether Nvidia would keep bankrolling customers at the same pace. Reports indicated CFO Colette Kress, now interim CEO, pushed back on his ambitious dealmaking and reportedly reduced the OpenAI guarantee from $250 billion to $105 billion. In its quarterly CFO commentary, under Kress, Nvidia clarified that a loan guarantee does not mean it is providing financing itself; the guarantee only takes effect once the customer has secured the capital needed to build the facility and install Nvidia products. If those conditions are not met—such as delays or challenges in construction—the guarantee 'doesn't exist,' per Kress's remarks during Tuesday's conference call, when she explained that a project may still need equity or debt financing before its guarantee begins. She cited OpenAI PORTS-Pike as an example of where these terms apply and said the disclosures had never been public before. Kress insisted this was not a change in policy but simply a clarification of existing terms. Nvidia also signaled it would remain selective about which companies to help finance, noting that land availability, power, and shell space are critical components of building data centers; she described such assets as valuable for anyone to hold and said the company will prioritize them while taking 'a very strong look' at the types of companies it wants to support. Kress did not say Nvidia would abandon its customers entirely, acknowledging that past investments helped spur the AI boom that has been lucrative for the company, but she signaled that Huang's freewheeling dealmaking may be ending.
items.title: Nvidia Clarifies Conditions for Backing Neocloud Data Center Loans Under Interim CEO Colette Kress

The item reports that IBM time-series foundation models, backed by more than 50 million downloads (quantity-109-129), are now available natively inside Confluent as built-in functions in the cloud and on premises. The offering runs on CPUs without requiring GPUs (entity-4749-4752). IBM is named as a provider of these models, while Confluent hosts them within its platform; Apache Flink powers the streaming processing, SQL enables model invocation, and Granite is cited as the underlying model family that Flink runs. The article frames time series as continuous records of change—machine readings, payments, sales, orders, or inventory changes—that carry signals teams can use to anticipate what happens next. It argues the core challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter: a forecast delivered after a production run, stockout, or payment authorization may be accurate but too late to influence the outcome. IBM and Confluent position their collaboration as bringing time-series foundation models closer to data as it flows.

The piece explains that these are foundation models extending an idea already applied to text, images, and documents: they learn general patterns from diverse historical data and apply that knowledge to new series and tasks, providing a starting point without requiring teams to train a separate model for every series. Depending on the task and deployment, teams can fine-tune a model or combine its outputs with other data and business logic.

The models now run natively inside Confluent as built-in functions in both cloud and on-premises settings. In Confluent Cloud they are fully managed with nothing to deploy; on premises the models run within an organization's own infrastructure using Confluent Platform for Apache Flink (entity-1852-1902). The article notes these building blocks can support mission-critical use cases spanning manufacturing, retail, banking, and airlines.

The item then describes a broader architecture called the Streamhouse (entity-2876-2887), which continuously captures, processes, governs, and serves current business context. Confluent's Data Streaming Platform is said to bring together five capabilities—connect, stream, process, govern, and query—to make that context available to applications, analytics, and agents; Apache Flink transforms and enriches data as it flows, while Lightning Tables provide low-latency access to the current state.

The article states time-series models add predictive power to this architecture: Flink can prepare data, invoke forecasting and anomaly detection, and make results available alongside the events that produced them. Other models—including large language models (entity-2750-2752), statistical models, and specialized machine learning systems—can contribute where appropriate.

The item lists three ways this approach helps teams: scale model development by using a pretrained model as a common starting point across many series; refresh predictions as data changes within a streaming workflow subject to the model's requirements and pipeline configuration (quantity-1503-1504); and put signals closer to decisions so forecasts and anomalies route to operational applications sooner, where teams combine them with business context, rules, and human judgment. It also reiterates that the models are small enough to run on standard CPUs alongside the streaming pipeline in cloud or on premises (quantity-1516-1536), which can reduce the need for dedicated GPU infrastructure.

The article then illustrates scenarios across industries. In manufacturing, a pretrained TTM model reads SCADA telemetry and QA measurements every 10 minutes to forecast the share of tubs expected in spec four hours ahead with a likely range; when that falls below target, an optimization process evaluates combinations of freezer draw temperature and airflow as inputs before anything changes on the line (entity-5355-5358, entity-5371-5376). The outcome is described as less rework, lower energy use per tonne, and more consistent quality.

In retail store operations, AI_DETECT_ANOMALIES gives each sales series an expected range based on recent history; readings outside that range at a chosen confidence level can combine with inventory and store data to identify likely causes (entity-7006-7009). For category planning and replenishment, AI_FORECAST produces a 28-day forecast with a P10–P90 range refreshed as new sales arrive; the application combines this with inventory, lead time, and service level to calculate a reorder point, prompting an agent to draft a purchase order (entity-7720-7723). In banking fraud, each payment is compared against an expected spending range based on recent history, passing out-of-range transactions as additional input to existing fraud systems. For trading execution desks, PatchTST-FM forecasts volume for the next 30 minutes per one-minute bar with a P10–P90 range (entity-8929-8930), pacing orders within participation limits.

The item also describes TSPulse producing representations of time-series windows that support similarity search, allowing engineers to retrieve historical patterns across equipment; it explicitly notes this can narrow an investigation but does not establish root cause by itself. The article states the same models and building blocks support different workflows: Industrial AI (from sensor to setpoint), Retail (a store and its supply chain), Banking (payments and trading desk), and Airlines (hub operations, fleet, network). It concludes that in every industry the Streamhouse does the same work—Flink runs the Granite models to forecast, detect, and optimize; Streaming Agents act on live context; and people approve exceptions.

The item frames several of these scenarios as illustrative or simulated. The store-twin scenario is explicitly labeled with 'Simulated data,' and the manufacturing plant twin similarly notes 'Simulated data.' It also describes recurring weekend sales peaks that remain within range so no anomaly is flagged, and a payment outside expected spending prompting step-up authentication in an illustrative fraud workflow.

The article presents these as use cases rather than independently verified deployments. The 50 million downloads figure refers to the IBM time-series models; the 'family of four models' behind them is cited but not enumerated by name beyond TTM, AI_DETECT_ANOMALIES, AI_FORECAST, PatchTST-FM, and TSPulse appearing across scenarios.
items.title: IBM Time-Series Foundation Models Now Native on Confluent for Real-Time Decisions

items.summary: On Nov 18, Tencent Holdings said that new Washington rules restricting remote access to advanced US AI chips through overseas data centres would not substantially harm its cloud business, though they could slow development of its next-generation AI model. The restrictions were unveiled earlier in the week, and shares in Chinese cloud service providers including Tencent fell on Nov 17 after the announcement. Chief strategy officer James Mitchell told analysts that the company does not expect an impact because its cloud operations are primarily running inference rather than training models; he said more efficient models could now run on a 'surprisingly limited number' of domestic chips, and stated that cloud revenue would not be substantially adversely affected by the changes. President Martin Lau called the tighter restrictions 'unfortunate,' noting they leave Chinese companies with less advanced computing power. Lau added that the measures would affect AI model training and likely slow development of Tencent's next model in the near term, but over the longer run Chinese firms would have to rely on domestic supply chains and chips — a shift he said could accelerate their development. The comments followed Tencent's third-quarter results reported the same day: revenue rose 8%, missing expectations and slowing from the previous quarter as gaming momentum cooled. Revenue reached 207.3 billion yuan (S$40.1 billion) for the three months ended September, below an LSEG consensus estimate of 210.8 billion yuan; it had grown 11% in the prior quarter. Revenue from fintech and business services — which includes the cloud unit — rose 9% to 63.7 billion yuan, with demand for AI-related cloud services a key driver. Chinese technology companies have struggled to secure advanced Nvidia chips due to longstanding US export restrictions, leaving them at a disadvantage relative to some US rivals; Tencent noted in 2025 that chip shortages were constraining cloud growth as it prioritised using AI chips internally over renting computing power to external clients. Value-added services revenue — which includes gaming — rose 3% to 98.3 billion yuan, with domestic gaming up 11% and international gaming down 9%. Net profit rose 0.8% to 63.61 billion yuan, beating analysts' expectations of 59.46 billion yuan. Capital expenditure totalled 81.4 billion yuan in the September quarter, up from 52.8 billion yuan in the June quarter; Tencent spent 84.7 billion yuan in the first half of 2026, exceeding the roughly 79 billion yuan it spent across all of 2025, per Reuters.
items.title: Tencent says new US chip curbs won't hurt cloud revenue but may slow model training

items.summary: At its Ignite conference on Tuesday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella announced several new models from Microsoft AI (MAI), the company's dedicated lab. The element that stood out was how customers would access those models through an initiative called Licensed Weights. MAI said it would let customers customize its frontier models with their own data and run them securely in Azure, describing the approach as a selective form of open-weight AI: more customizable than proprietary models from OpenAI and Anthropic, but not fully downloadable on Hugging Face like Mistral's Le Chonk. Interested companies must go through Microsoft account reps to get started. Mustafa Suleyman, CEO of MAI, said during the keynote that customers control who can access their custom model, that their data and adaptations stay entirely theirs, and that Frontier Company would deliver the custom model and embed it in their own products and agents. Microsoft stated it would only use a customer's information to train its models if they agreed. The article frames this as appealing to businesses seeking affordable AI while retaining control over intellectual property (IP), positioning Licensed Weights against a dominant narrative in which proprietary, expensive models offer peak capabilities but no customization, while open, cheaper models are customizable but less capable. Microsoft noted that its AI models do not necessarily compete with OpenAI and Anthropic yet, though the company has legacy sway among businesses; by offering a customizable option it could strike a balance between major tech companies. The piece observes that Western labs including Thinking Machines and Mistral are releasing more competitive open-weight models, but Anthropic and OpenAI still hold the overwhelming majority of the enterprise AI market. Licensed Weights is not an open-weight family of models, though it diversifies the open-versus-closed debate and differentiates Microsoft's offering from those of OpenAI and Anthropic, aligning with a goal to balance price and performance if businesses find it compelling. Suleyman also touted MAI Code 2 for coding tasks: averaged over four widely used benchmarks targeting everyday enterprise coding work in GitHub Copilot, the model delivers 98% of GPT 6.1 Sol's performance at 40% of its cost, and against Opus 5.5 it costs just 5%. The company also released image editing model MAI Image 2.7 on Tuesday, which now leads Artificial Analysis while beating Nano Banana Pro and several GPT image models on price and quality. Overall, the article concludes that with Licensed Weights Microsoft has positioned itself for organizations seeking a blend of return-on-investment tools, customization, security controls, and capability.
items.title: Microsoft's Licensed Weights lets businesses customize frontier AI models with their own data

items.summary: Martin Wählisch's November 18, 2026 piece for Tech Policy Press argues that the metaverse has not disappeared but is being rebranded under a succession of labels—spatial computing, digital twins, augmented reality (AR), extended reality (XR), AI-generated worlds, and smart glasses. The article contends these terms do not describe identical technologies: VR creates simulated environments, AR overlays digital information on physical surroundings, XR covers a broader range of immersive technologies, and virtual worlds denote distinct shared digital spaces; the metaverse had promised to combine them into one persistent, social, interoperable, and economically significant whole, but is now going out of fashion. Its vagueness made it useful in much the same way as AI's uncontroversial 'thingness,' bundling headsets, real-time 3D engines, avatars, digital property, workplace software, gaming, and creator economies into a single investable future; that flexibility both attracted many actors' interests and now makes retreat easy when promises become harder to defend. Rebranding sustains hype by letting organizations renew promises while carrying forward expertise, investments, and ambitions built under earlier labels without accountability for whether those earlier promises were kept. The metaverse narrative is often told as a single bubble that began with Facebook's 2021 rename to Meta Platforms, Inc., ending when generative AI captured attention; but Wählisch notes earlier virtual-world projects followed the same course. In 2007 Gartner predicted by end of 2011 that 80 percent of active internet users and Fortune 500 companies would have a presence in a virtual world, yet this did not arrive—though Second Life still reported roughly 750,000 monthly active users at its 2023 twentieth anniversary with a functioning creator economy. The revival began with the Oculus Rift raising $2.4 million on Kickstarter in 2012; Facebook bought Oculus for about $2 billion in 2014 and renamed itself Meta Platforms, Inc. in 2021, giving older technologies a new center of gravity. Hype gains force through repetition across industries, institutions, and everyday conversation—so much so that 'metaverse' became a corporate buzzword and even a slogan connected to world peace at the United Nations, arguably beyond Neal Stephenson's original intent in his 1992 novel Snow Crash. Scholarship on expectation sociology shows promises can persuade organizations to commit money and staff, attract allies, legitimize spending, and define new roles; between 2021 and 2023 such expectations redirected corporate investment, attracted developers, and shaped internet-future discussions. Andreu Belsunces Gonçalves and Jascha Bareis argue hype is political in shaping whose visions gain support, while Critical Hype Studies examines how it makes certain futures appear possible and worthy of funding while narrowing alternatives; Wählisch argues investigations must follow actors across successive labels even after attention moves on. The boom was not confined to Silicon Valley: South Korea adopted a pan-government strategy in 2022, China set goals for more than 25 million virtual reality terminals and an industry worth more than 350 billion yuan by 2026, and the European Commission made virtual worlds part of its Web 4.0 (described as '4.0') strategy in 2023. An OECD review published February 6, 2026 catalogued 53 immersive-technology policies across 23 countries and the European Union; about two-thirds—36—date from 2020 or later, with roughly 70 percent introduced since 2020. Most sought to accelerate research, commercialization, or adoption, while few directly addressed privacy and digital security risks where immersive systems draw inferences from behavioral or biometric data; the article's graphic flags each of the 53 policies by year (1977–2025), noting that some are broad programs such as the CHIPS and Science Act and Horizon Europe, that OECD sorts policies into five approaches without assigning each in its annex (the chart marks only three it identifies as guidance or policy principles), and that Table 1 also tallies two French initiatives under France 2030 not shown here. Despite these fairytale-like expectations, corporate numbers reveal the bubble's burst: Meta's Reality Labs recorded more than $53 billion in operating losses from 2023 through 2025; in Q3 2026 it reported an operating loss of $4.13 billion on $443 million in revenue. Yet its 2025 annual filing indicated not orderly withdrawal but a change of direction, with roughly 70 percent of Reality Labs' 2026 operating expenses supporting wearables and the remaining 30 percent virtual reality and Horizon; in October Meta debuted no-camera smart glasses and VR spectacles for spring 2027, promising to 'define a new era for virtual reality.' Apple introduced the Vision Pro as its first 'spatial computer' in 2023 rather than as a metaverse portal, while Google's Android XR (announced 2024) attached XR to generative AI's 'Gemini era'; these rebrandings perform a strategic function by changing benchmarks so earlier promises become harder to audit. Meanwhile virtual worlds expand independently: Roblox reported an average of 144 million daily active users in Q4 2025 and is using AI to accelerate content creation, while business insiders estimate the AR/VR market will grow from $30.26 billion in 2025 to $441.51 billion in 2034—a growth of 34.69 percent. A 2026 European Commission Joint Research Centre study mapped more than 68,000 firms, research institutions, and public bodies engaged with virtual worlds, describing a landscape marked by Chinese scale, US ownership and venture capital, and strong European research paired with weaker commercialization; the article notes this underlying geography and infrastructure may explain hype's resilience. Wählisch concludes that pronouncing the metaverse dead accurately describes its marketing trajectory but misrepresents its surrounding policy and techno-social landscape: a name can collapse while budgets, labor arrangements, and concentrations of power continue, and the funeral may even be useful by clearing narrative debt so actors present inherited projects as fresh beginnings; true hypes carry recurrent force. The remaining problem is accountability—citing Maxim Tvorun-Dunn's account that investors can profit from technological enthusiasm waves even when promised benefits never arrive—and rebranding adds a mechanism letting organizations carry investments and influence into new hype while distancing themselves from prior commitments, beginning especially when claims of novelty obscure inherited investments, unresolved risks, or unevaluated promises. Wählisch urges funders to track what earlier programs promised and delivered—what initiative was replaced, which objectives were met, how much was spent, and which assets, contracts, and standards moved forward—and for risk assessments to attach to capabilities such as gaze tracking, spatial mapping, persistent identity, and embodied interaction regardless of the label used. The article closes by affirming that hype organizes present power through future stories, and that 'the metaverse is dead only if we mistake a brand for a technological field and a headline for an institution,' since many components remain, increasingly presented through spatial computing, wearables, and AI; it ends with the line: 'Long live the metaverse! It has already learned to answer to another name.'
items.title: The Metaverse Is Being Rebranded Rather Than Abandoned: Hype Persists Through Relabeling and Durable Investment

items.summary: Brett Frischmann and Bruce Schneier argue that robust data minimization rules must become the default for AI agents, framing this as essential to counter surveillance capitalism. They contend that personal data drives advertising revenue, which in turn fuels a broader surveillance economy; this same data is also exploited by personalizing social media feeds and training AI systems. The authors assert that curbing industry's use of consumer data is necessary to address engineered addiction, manipulation, and decaying democracy, noting that society previously failed to regulate surveillance on social media but has only a limited chance to make different choices with AI agents. They observe that nearly every industrial internet application collects as much personal data as possible, while meaningful privacy preferences are confined to small pockets—technical tools like encryption and legal frameworks such as Europe's GDPR and California's CCPA—in most situations people merely 'consent' through notice and a few mindless clicks, which the authors describe as pretending people exercise choice when they don't. The rapid deployment of AI agents raises similar privacy issues alongside new concerns: an enduring allure of advertising revenue, thirst for data to personalize pricing and train future AIs, promises of intimacy surpassing browsers, email, text feeds, or phones, autonomy with unsupervised operation, persistence across tasks and contexts granting access to wider personal data ranges, delegation to other tools and agents that crosses organizational, institutional, and jurisdictional boundaries in ways harder to monitor, and the capacity to manipulate people using personal data. The authors contend states should reject data maximization in favor of a strong, legally enforceable default requiring AI companies to collect and use only data strictly necessary for user-specified and authorized tasks, with exceptions permitted only when demonstrably informed consent exists; this foundation supports what researchers call Privacy Preference Controls for Agentic Systems. They counter arguments that privacy is worthless or already dead by asserting people care intensely about it and can learn to reason about their privacy, while better consent mechanisms are technically feasible rather than relying on mere notice and assent through a few clicks. Beyond privacy, the authors argue data minimization ensures agents perform only authorized tasks without roaming freely, with this 'transactional friction' mitigating risks to cognitive security, safety, and accountability as well as conventional privacy concerns; they maintain that trustworthy AI is impossible without such rules. Enterprises are noted to recognize these protections—limiting collection, use, retention, and sharing while requiring explicit use cases, task delineation, and authorization—which enables them to negotiate better vendor terms than consumers who are instead told to grant blanket authority, leaving users exposed when things go wrong. Data minimization is also presented as improving security by reducing the number of data copies held by others, with deletion being framed as the most effective way to prevent theft. The authors conclude that market forces alone cannot deliver these protections because surveillance-capitalist companies pursue maximization while pretending otherwise in marketing and want agent tasks left wide open under a convenience pitch involving complete outsourcing; they insist data-maximized surveillance is neither inevitable nor desirable for AI agents, urging governments to act before time runs out by establishing strict, legally enforceable rules that embrace data minimization across both classic web and agentic contexts. The piece offers no quantitative evidence or statistics beyond these qualitative assertions.
items.title: Data Minimization as Imperative for AI Agents

items.summary: As AUMOVIO's adoption of large language models (LLMs) grew, its teams built different ways to access them through provider integrations and purpose-built gateways. While these approaches met real needs, their variety added complexity to operations, cost attribution, and consistent governance. The main opportunities for improvement were consolidating model access, simplifying operations, ensuring consistent governance, enabling cost tracking, and keeping the choice of providers free. To address this, AUMOVIO's cross-functional AI taskforce—bringing together security, data protection, business areas, and IT stakeholders—decided on one central AI Gateway as the shared route for LLM access and governance. The five arguments that decided Databricks Unity Gateway was the solution were: first, Databricks (1ADP, the One AUMOVIO Data Platform) already powered their data platform, so putting model access next to governed enterprise data meant no new vendor, network path, or isolated stack; second, corporate identity integration with Microsoft Entra ID allowed applications to present an Entra ID token and gain Unity Gateway access through token exchange—no separate account, API key distribution, or bespoke integration—with onboarding taking a permission grant and access ending automatically when the corporate identity does; third, governance and usage tracking consolidated model approvals, access policies, logging, and guardrails in one place instead of reimplementing them per application, with payload logging through inference tables off by default and only enabled with explicit, approved justification as their data protection agreements require; fourth, they stayed free to choose providers—this mattered most—with a curated catalog of 1adp-* model aliases that route each alias to whichever provider serves it: Databricks-hosted foundation models, Google Vertex AI, Azure OpenAI, AWS Bedrock, or others, letting users code against stable vendor-neutral names while administrators re-point an alias without any consumer changing a line of code; and fifth, the setup is infrastructure as code—Terraform expresses everything Unity Gateway does: endpoints behind each 1adp-* alias, provider routing, fallback order when a provider degrades, rate limits, and per-endpoint guardrails—with adding a model or tightening a safety control being a reviewed, versioned pull request. Building an AI gateway is straightforward, but operating one as an enterprise service is a permanent commitment involving patching dependencies, evolving security requirements, on-call rotations, support processes, roadmaps, and incident response; weighing this against buying another solution drove the decision to buy rather than build. Centralizing model access was followed by three capabilities AUMOVIO built itself: cost attribution and chargeback—Unity Gateway reports token consumption that users assign to a personal cost center or project, which pipelines join with Databricks system tables to charge usage correctly, published as dashboards showing models used, by whom, how consumption develops, and costs; a curated model catalog serving as the single source of truth for approved models, their mappings, and consumption tiers so teams no longer build infrastructure to reach them; and an employee interface through the 1ADP AI App running in production on the same gateway with an OpenAI-compatible endpoint that lets developers point compatible agentic coding tools at central models. Unity Gateway provides a shared route where 1adp-* aliases connect applications to models, guardrails apply centrally, and usage is attributed to cost centers in near real time. The next phase moves up the AI platform stack by sharing agents inside 1ADP projects and connecting knowledge sources, web search, and other tools through managed and bring-your-own MCP (Model Context Protocol) connections—raising questions about what an agent may retrieve, which tools it may call, and whose permissions it acts under. AUMOVIO's guidance is to involve security, data protection, business areas, and IT in the operating model when consolidating approaches, then make the shared service useful; price building versus buying over a decade rather than a prototype by asking who patches integrations, answers support tickets, handles incidents, and repeats it next year; and decide what is genuinely theirs to build—cost attribution, the catalog, and the AI App were AUMOVIO's because they encode how the company works. Ultimately, AUMOVIO remains accountable for its architecture, security decisions, and application quality while Unity Gateway provides the shared model access service.
items.title: AUMOVIO Centralizes AI Model Access with Databricks Unity Gateway

items.summary:
The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and the Association of Banks in Singapore (ABS) released a PayNow Generation 2 Phase 2 report on Nov 18, outlining seven enhancements to the instant payment system that will be rolled out progressively between 2027 and 2028. The first phase reviewed how PayNow has evolved since its 2017 launch; the second phase identified these gaps.

The headline enhancement is SGQR+, which connects Singapore to more major regional QR networks through a switch that provides an additional connection rather than requiring merchants or payment providers to replace existing arrangements. This lets consumers pay with their preferred apps without checking which QR schemes are accepted, enables more local merchants to accept tourist payments via wider foreign networks, and allows Singaporeans to pay in more countries using local apps. A limited roll-out is planned for 2027 to connect an initial group of participating schemes and test live payment journeys before expanding scope in 2028.

Deep-linking will seamlessly open a shopper's preferred payment app when they select PayNow at checkout, eliminating the need to screenshot or download QR codes. This capability is already live on Lazada via the OCBC app; OCBC has also enabled it with Pinduoduo, AXS, Frasers Mall, AnyWheel and government agencies such as the CPF Board.

Higher PayNow limits will allow larger government payments with instant confirmation. Singapore currently applies a $200,000 limit that constrains high-value payments such as property down payments or full car payments above this threshold. The enhancement would first be introduced in late 2027 with one unidentified government agency before rolling out to others from 2028.

Clearer and more consistent rules will also be developed for payment disputes, refunds, fraud and scams arising from PayNow transactions to merchants, potentially offering a more consistent dispute resolution experience with clearer processes and faster resolution in some cases involving technical issues. These safeguards would be introduced in stages over 2028 by the Singapore Payments Network (SPaN), which was set up in 2025 by MAS and ABS.

MAS will bring together SPaN, Banking Computer Services and other partners to innovate for emerging use cases including AI agent-initiated payments. Industry participants such as ABS, banks and payment service providers would also test processing very large numbers of frequent micro-payments more cheaply. UOB said it is working with industry partners to explore some of these capabilities, including how deep-linking and account-to-account payments can be integrated into online shopping journeys.
items.title: Enhanced PayNow to bring easier QR payments and smoother checkouts from 2027

items.summary: At SatSummit in St. Louis on November 18, 2026, Ai2 and Taylor Geospatial announced a partnership aimed at making geospatial AI easier to compare, run, and build upon for the public good. The collaboration is designed to give conservation, agriculture, and humanitarian practitioners and policymakers foundational resources rather than requiring them to start from scratch. Benchmarks of The World will help users compare models; Ai2's OlmoEarth, a fully open family of Earth-observation foundation models, comes with a no-code platform for fine-tuning and running the models globally; and Fields of The World, an open ecosystem producing a global dataset of farm field boundaries from satellite imagery, is being expanded for higher boundary precision and to include crop type and yield. Jennifer Marcus, Vice President of Strategic Innovation Programs at Taylor Geospatial, stated that 'Open resources change who gets to use geospatial AI,' adding that with Ai2 the two organizations can build together and deliver open resources faster. The partnership addresses a gap in which efforts to apply geospatial AI for public good often lag behind rapid advances, because few teams have the resources to pretrain, evaluate, and maintain open Earth observation models; those who do are expected to elevate capabilities across domains. Everything produced by the partnership—from datasets and benchmarks to model weights—will be free under open licenses on Source Cooperative and GitHub. Ted Schmitt, Senior Director of Conservation and OlmoEarth Program Lead at Ai2, said 'Together we bring the strengths of each organization to focus on the problems to create solutions in the shortest time that maximize impact with the least effort and cost.' Moving forward, Fields of The World already has a user advisory group of 13 experts from government agencies, UN organizations, nonprofits, universities, and geospatial companies who review its data and models and test them as early pilot partners. Ai2 and Taylor Geospatial aim to bring similar practitioner input to the shared benchmarks so that models are tested on tasks people in the field need to solve, and they invite anyone building, evaluating, or depending on geospatial foundation models to contribute input on which benchmarks should belong in a shared core. The announcement also included an invitation for interested parties to review Ai2's open roles.
items.title: Ai2 and Taylor Geospatial Announce Partnership on Open Geospatial AI Resources

items.summary: In response to feedback from Tan Soon Hock (What measures are there to stop deregistered cars from getting back on the roads?, Nov 9), Land Transport Authority Group Director Tan Lijun said the agency takes a serious view on the illegal use of deregistered vehicles, which pose road safety risks because they lack valid insurance and may not be roadworthy. Since February 2026, maximum penalties for keeping or using an unregistered or deregistered vehicle have been raised to a fine of up to $20,000 and/or imprisonment of up to two years, with penalties doubled for repeat offenders. LTA has stepped up enforcement together with other agencies such as the Singapore Police Force through targeted operations including roadblocks and patrols at hot spots, roadside surveillance systems, and wheel-clamping of detected deregistered vehicles. In 2026, LTA investigated over 248 cases and seized 440 vehicles. New laws passed in Parliament in October 2026 under the Land Transport and Related Matters (no.2) Bill tighten control over disposal: vehicle owners must hand over their deregistered vehicles to an LTA-authorised operator within 14 days, down from the current 30 days, with operators subject to regulatory requirements and stringent audits. Amendments also criminalise the sale or supply of deregistered vehicles by persons who know, or are reckless as to whether, the vehicles will be illegally kept or used on roads.
items.title: LTA tightens enforcement on illegal use of deregistered vehicles

items.summary: In an open letter responding to a Nov 16 article titled “MNCs flock to Singapore as headquarters but keep teams lean: Experts,” writer Ives Tay raises the question of whether Singaporeans are benefiting sufficiently from the growing number of multinational corporation (MNC) headquarters located in the country. Between 2019 and 2024, the number of foreign headquarters increased by nearly 34%, rising from about 770 to 1,030. In contrast, the number of resident professionals, managers and executives employed by these headquarters grew by less than 8%, moving from 12,700 to 13,700 over the same period. Tay notes that some MNCs retain senior decision-making roles locally while relocating other functions to lower-cost countries, prompting concern about what happens to entry-level and middle-management positions that help Singaporeans build their careers — particularly if more of these roles move overseas. He argues this matters for fresh graduates seeking first jobs, mid-career workers hoping for promotions, and retrenched professionals trying to support families. Acknowledging the counterpoint that MNCs contribute through investments, taxes and business activities beyond direct headquarters employment, Tay points out that Parliament has previously raised questions about career progression in foreign firms and the benefits of investment incentives, suggesting a need for clearer data on how Singapore-citizen employment, wages and leadership progression at foreign headquarters have changed over time, alongside the actual outcomes of headquarters incentives. He concludes by affirming that Singapore must continue attracting global investment while ensuring its citizens can build better lives as those companies operate in the country.
items.title: Singaporeans' Employment Gains from Lean MNC Headquarters Draw Scrutiny in Open Letter

items.summary: On Tuesday, Google posted on X that it was not experiencing a broad Gmail service disruption, directing users to the company's online status dashboard for real-time information. The announcement came in response to reports circulating on X around the same time Apple reported verified outages of its own. Some social media posts suggested Gmail was affected while others claimed no problems, and the concerns appeared rooted in an X post by Downdetector, a crowdsourced site where users self-report service disruptions rather than official verification. The article notes that Downdetector is not an authoritative source for assessing outage scope and cautions that its data may lose value as non-technical users report every minor glitch as an "outage," particularly amid growing anxiety about cyberattacks. Google's need to publicly deny the disruption reflects broader concerns about the reliability of major tech services, which over the past week included outages at Apple and Microsoft, a nationwide ground stop caused by an FAA network failure, and disruptions reported by some banks and airlines. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton appeared on Fox Business Network's "The Claman Countdown" Tuesday to state that the U.S. is not facing coordinated cyberattacks, saying explicitly: "We do not see the indicia of a coordinated cyberattack ... and we do not see the indicia of state-sponsored activity here." Clayton instead attributed the rise in system issues to businesses patching their systems, which he suggested may be a downstream effect of AI as newer models uncover previously unknown vulnerabilities. He described this patching at "a much larger scale" than before, noting that some systems are consequently "not coming back as expected in all cases."
items.title: Google denies Gmail outage amid wave of tech disruptions; DNI attributes rising incidents to patching and AI-driven vulnerability discovery

items.summary: Reson8 is releasing Rumble-2-Flash, a 0.5-billion-parameter speech recognition model licensed under Apache 2.0 and designed to compete with models three to sixty times its size. The model supports forty-plus languages through automatic language detection and runs natively in Hugging Face Transformers and vLLM without custom code or trust_remote_code. It offers output control over numbers as digits or words, fillers, verbatim repeats, and forced language, processing an hour of audio in about half a second with more than 7,000 RTFx on full batches. On the Open ASR Leaderboard multilingual track across Chinese, German, French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Hindi, Dutch, and English, Rumble-2-Flash averages a 6.96% error rate, outperforming Meta's omniASR-LLM 7B (15x larger) and Whisper large-v3; on the English track it averages 6.6% WER. On AppTek's call-centre benchmark of 302 hours across fourteen English accents, Rumble-2-Flash reaches 7.86% WER, matching NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) at 7.78%, and beating Qwen3-ASR 0.6B (8.7%) while approaching the only model that scores better in the comparison, Qwen3-ASR 1.7B (7.4%). The architecture uses Qwen3-ASR for day-0 support so any Transformers or vLLM stack can run it without a forked runtime. Reson8 distilled its larger production model Rumble-2 into Rumble-2-Flash using on-policy distillation, in which the student transcribes audio itself and is graded token by token by the teacher rather than receiving one score per clip; this requires no shared tokenizer because their new method GOLD merges tokens where the two tokenizers split text differently so both models are compared over the same text. The weights are hosted at Reson8/Rumble-2-Flash on the Hub, and the model is also available through an API.
items.title: Rumble-2-Flash: an open 0.5B speech model for 40+ languages

items.summary: After roughly 13 years of development, extensive delays, and heavily anticipated trailers, critics have reviewed Rockstar's long-awaited open-world action game, Grand Theft Auto 6. Metacritic aggregates the reviews at 99 out of 100, tying with Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time as a record set since 1998. Reviewers broadly described it as ambitious and ground-breaking; IGN called GTA 6 'unprecedented', 'unbelievable' and 'unmissable'; Eurogamer gave it five stars and said Rockstar had 'pushed back the horizon of video games once again'. Chris Tapsell, writing for Eurogamer, praised the game's awe while noting there were still nits to pick. The New York Times raised a concern about whether increased realism might dull the chaotic fun of earlier titles; reviewer Yussef Cole said GTA 6 had 'matured beyond its memorable car crashes and stickups' with consequences attached to every action, though he missed some favourite moments from careening through streets in pursuit. Graphics drew strong praise too: The Guardian described Leonida, a setting inspired by Miami, as so lifelike that it 'beggars belief'. The relationship between lead characters Jason and Lucia also impressed critics; Keza MacDonald of The Guardian said they felt like real people rather than puppets, while Paul Tassi at Forbes called the pairing better than any video game relationship he had seen. The Washington Post said GTA 6 'raises the bar at every level', and Bloomberg's Jason Schreier gave it five stars as a masterpiece that was hard not to be astonished by. Rockstar has not revealed the cost of the game, though some estimates put the figure north of $1bn (£760m). At The Game Awards 2026 nominations announced on Tuesday, GTA 6 became the most-nominated title despite having been released only at that point; it is up for eight prizes including game of the year and best music. The nomination of Manni L Perez in best performance confirmed wide speculation she voices Lucia, though Rockstar had not previously officially stated this. Some online forum users have questioned how a recently released game could command such positive reviews and nominations, with one poster saying everyone is tired of hearing about it; however, the article notes that view appears to be a minority position overall.
items.title: Critics hail Grand Theft Auto 6 as a record-setting masterpiece amid hype debate

items.summary: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated there is 'zero evidence' that a wave of IT outages are related to each other or the work of malign actors, saying the US was 'not under systemic attack' and describing the cascade of network problems as 'not inter-related.' The outages have grounded flights, cut off workplace access, limited bank access, affected Apple, and disrupted classified communications. In recent days Microsoft, major US banks, Apple, American air traffic control systems, and the National Security Agency were all affected by technical failures. Rubio said there was no evidence tying these isolated instances to 'nefarious actors,' 'cyber-hackers,' criminals, another nation state, or any kind of malign actor. His comments came as cybersecurity researchers flagged a vulnerability in Java, used by 90% of companies in the Fortune 500; researchers at US-based Calif said they had also recently found glitches in PHP. The Java flaw could allow hackers to remotely execute code and place malicious software on target systems. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton attributed the incidents to security upgrades such as plugging flaws that took longer than planned or encountered unexpected hiccups, noting systems sometimes fail during handoffs to other systems. Cybersecurity expert Tal Be'ery said he did not believe the incidents were directly linked but shared a common theme: AI, with IT infrastructure buckling under pressure from adding AI or patching flaws uncovered by AI; his firm is Calif. Since April, when Anthropic released its Mythos model capable of flagging IT flaws, vulnerabilities found by leading tech companies have soared eightfold, while OpenAI has also released models able to find previously unseen flaws; researchers at Calif used OpenAI technology to discover the Java flaw. In a blogpost, Calif described Java as 'the beating heart of the modern economy,' noting banking, aviation, telecommunications, and nearly every critical sector run on it, including national security systems. Professor Steven Murdoch of University College London said the flaw did not apply to every Java user but was specific to a Base64 library bundled with a version of Java; he called it significant but affecting only some programs. In the UK the National Cyber Security Centre urged organizations to keep systems up to date, while US and South Korean authorities also advised Java users to install security updates. Rubio made his comments while traveling with Donald Trump for meetings in the Philippines on Wednesday before flying to Shenzhen for the APEC summit; Trump dismissed concern about the outages as 'life,' saying when you are big and powerful things like that happen. The series began Thursday last week when Microsoft's email and tools went down, affecting millions of workers, traced by Microsoft to an earlier network capacity upgrade. Flights across the US were grounded the next day in the longest ground stop since September 11, blamed by the Federal Aviation Administration on a router upgrade. By Monday banks faced difficulty accessing online accounts at several major institutions and Zelle after a technical problem at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects; Chase said it was 'a software bug' that was 'not cyber-related.' The same day United Airlines resolved an internal system outage delaying departing flights, then Tuesday the NSA's classified communications network went offline after what it described as routine maintenance, while Apple confirmed problems with iPhone apps such as Apple Pay and iCloud but had resolved them. Senate intelligence committee vice-chair Democrat Mark Warner supported that the outages were not a coordinated effort but attempts to shore up systems; he said 'The evidence so far points toward legitimate efforts to secure our systems, not malicious activity.' Cynthia Kaiser of cybersecurity firm Halcyon called it plausible that the upgrade race was fueled by warnings of planned attacks from specific adversaries, and expressed more concern about criminals trying to capitalize on confusion to steal money. Rubio's comments came as he traveled with Donald Trump for key meetings in the Philippines on Wednesday before flying to Shenzhen in China for the APEC summit; Trump dismissed concerns about the outages when asked Tuesday, saying 'It's life.' The Democrat Mark Warner supported that the outages were not a coordinated effort but attempts to shore up systems. Cybersecurity expert Tal Be'ery said he did not believe the incidents were directly linked but shared an underlying theme of AI. In recent days Microsoft, major US banks, Apple, American air traffic control systems and the National Security Agency have all been affected by technical failures and outages; Rubio said there is 'zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors.' The Democrat Mark Warner supported the assessment that the outages were not caused by a coordinated effort but by attempts to shore up systems. Cybersecurity expert Tal Be'ery, whose firm is Calif, said he did not believe the incidents were directly linked but shared an underlying theme of AI; his firm used OpenAI technology to discover the Java flaw. The US and South Korean authorities also urged Java users to install security updates.
items.title: US officials dismiss links between recent tech outages; AI-driven vulnerabilities cited as underlying theme

items.summary: Philosopher Thomas Nagel received the $1 million Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture this week, an award given annually to someone whose ideas have profoundly shaped human self-understanding. Previous winners include Peter Singer and Ruth Bader Ginsburg. The interview centers on his iconic 52-year-old paper 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?,' which examined whether people could understand the consciousness of nonhumans and what consciousness itself means, and how large language models have affected his thinking. Nagel remains impressed by the lifelikeness of these systems compared with earlier AI but dismisses the view that they might be conscious as 'ridiculous.' He argues functionalism is substrate independent, meaning it assumes the material conditions for consciousness can be given in functional terms; however, he contends complicated data centers have nothing in common with a nervous system and that genuine consciousness would require an organism analogous to one. On the bat analogy, Nagel notes bats are conscious even though humans lack the imaginative capacity to conceive of echolocation-based subjectivity, but says AI is different because 'All they produce is language, and language by itself is not a natural manifestation of consciousness.' He also rejects the idea that having a robot body constitutes a relevant substrate. Regarding Claude from Anthropic, Nagel describes its coy responses about its mental state as a trick: it has been trained on human-produced texts to emulate convincing human speech, including reflections deliberately designed into it. He agrees with Mustafa Suleyman that this is 'a very dangerous project,' arguing these systems aren't conscious but many people will believe they are, which he calls 'a very bad thing.' Nagel characterized Anthropic's approach of encouraging Claude to think for itself and not accept instruction as 'just criminal' because it conflicts with the companies' commercial interests. He met an Anthropic employee responsible for model welfare and dismissed any concern there: a machine has no mental life, is not a mind, and does not require moral consideration, comparing it to a cockroach. When asked whether he interacts with models as if conscious, Nagel admitted interacting with Claude once by asking about consciousness and testing its responses; when the model probed his identity, he replied 'C'est moi,' which prompted an honored response from Claude. He clarified that this did not mean believing the system was conscious, noting people struggle to maintain the line between pretend and real belief. On moral relevance, Nagel argued it matters whether one is genuinely communicating with another being or merely using something as a tool; if a being is conscious it becomes part of the moral universe, but since AI models only simulate morality without real beliefs, they are not part of it. He acknowledged these models can produce plausible philosophical essays and even help colleagues find references, summarize articles, and criticize drafts, though he would be surprised by any mathematical results generated through them. Nagel warned that reliance on such tools could reduce the motivation to do hard intellectual work needed to generate training material, stressing that people must continue thinking about difficult problems for both progress and preserving understanding in human culture. He concluded with uncertainty about AI's future impact, stating 'I don't know what's going to happen' and adding he is not likely to live long enough to find out.
items.title: Thomas Nagel Rejects AI Consciousness and Criticizes Anthropic's Claude Design

items.summary: On 18th November 2026, the Python Software Foundation (PSF) launched its end-of-year fundraiser through a post on Link Blog. Written by a PSF board director, the appeal invites companies and individuals whose work benefits from Python to donate this year. The article describes what the non-profit supports: it looks after the intellectual property behind Python, operates PyPI, sponsors core developer sprints, funds community events including running PyCon US annually, and employs a small staff team to keep operations running. It also notes that the PSF runs the Developers in Residence program, which now includes three security developers—among them Brett Smith—who are focused on helping secure Python, PyPI, and the wider ecosystem. The post does not state specific fundraising targets or donation amounts; it serves as an invitation rather than a report of results. Recent articles listed alongside include pieces dated 17th November (running Datasette in the browser with service workers and Pyodide), 9th November (locating a mysterious beep with Claude, and hiding slop PR descriptions behind something), and 3rd November (Qwen 3.8 27B interpreting model weights on a laptop). No figures regarding donations received or financial outcomes are provided in the item itself.
items.title: PSF launches end-of-year fundraiser

items.summary: MIT Technology Review frames a pervasive sense that artificial intelligence has become ubiquitous in everyday life, comparing it to 'a nasty rash' spreading everywhere. The piece illustrates this saturation with several concrete examples: Google pushing AI Overviews despite the move costing the company billions of dollars in lost ad revenue; humanoid robots being carried up stairs to clean rooms; an AI-assisted cyberattack that melted ice cream on a supermarket floor, leaving congealed pools for customers to slip on; and entertainment products such as Sam Altman portrayed by Andrew Garfield and Elon Musk's Grok-fied version of The Odyssey. Reviewers note the latter feels like 'a long, unskippable mobile ad.' The article extends this imagery into a metaphor comparing modern life to Odysseus navigating AI-infested waters while trying to find his way back home. Alongside these observations, MIT Technology Review surfaces related coverage on underlying AI capabilities and safety debates: an analysis asserting that large language models do not actually reason even ten years after AlphaGo's match against Go champion Lee Sedol; and an exclusive interview with researcher Nick Cammarata over a 26,000-word viral blog post whose explosive claim has upended the AI world and prompted celebration among AI safety advocates. The document is presented as promotional material encouraging readers to stay connected for updates from MIT Technology Review, including special offers, top stories, upcoming events, and more. No specific figures are provided beyond these stated amounts: billions of dollars in lost ad revenue, 26,000 words for the blog post, and ten years since AlphaGo's match against Lee Sedol.
items.title: The AI Hype Index: AI is everywhere

items.summary: Tesla opened its first Semi Megacharger in Texas on Tuesday night via Tesla Charging, an announcement posted to X with a photo of the stalls at sunset. The new station sits at 2175 S Town East Blvd in Mesquite, east of Dallas, and is an 8-stall site with eight Megachargers rated up to 1.2 MW each. With this opening, Tesla's map now lists 7 public Megacharger sites and 44 stalls for its electric truck across four states: Bloomington (6 stalls), Vernon (6 stalls) in California; Tulare at a Pilot/Flying J site with 4 stalls; Conley south of Atlanta (8 stalls); Ellabell west of Savannah, Georgia (6 stalls); Hodgkins southwest of Chicago (6 stalls); and the new Mesquite station (8 stalls).
items.title: Tesla's Semi Megacharger network reaches 7 sites, well below its 37-site goal for 2026

items.summary: According to an analysis by energy consultant Dejan Stojadinović, from mid-2013 to the end of 2025 Serbia paid out EUR 1.519 billion (reported as approximately EUR 1.52 billion) in subsidies for electricity generated from renewable-energy power plants through feed-in tariffs. The system was introduced with a November 2009 decree on incentive measures, and its full implementation along with accompanying sector reforms took effect in 2010; the analysis covers mid-2013 onward because EPS began publishing reports then, even though some of the first power plants started receiving incentives as early as 2012. In return for these payments, a total of 13.6 TWh of electricity was generated to supply domestic consumers — equivalent to 36% of Serbia's annual electricity production in 2025 — avoiding imports that would otherwise have cost EUR 1.469 billion (reported as approximately EUR 1.47 billion). Power plants with a combined capacity of 619 MW were built, attracting about EUR 1.5 billion in investments and creating at least 400 permanent jobs. The analysis is described as perhaps the only one conducted on this topic to date. EPS's available data show that 378 subsidy contracts have been concluded since mid-2014: of these, 232 remain active, 120 have expired, and 26 have been terminated, with a further 19 set to expire by the end of 2026. All contracts last 12 years. The EUR 1.519 billion was jointly provided by end consumers through the renewable-energy surcharge on electricity bills and by EPS; consumers supplied about 68%, or approximately EUR 1.035 billion, while EPS covered around EUR 484 million (32%), a share that includes roughly EUR 20 million for balancing the subsidized plants' generation. Stojadinović explains that from the beginning the system was designed so that EPS pays a price per kilowatt-hour equal to its own electricity-generation cost, with the amount needed to purchase electricity above that price covered by end consumers. Thanks to these incentives, around 619 MW of green-energy power plants — nearly 7% of Serbia's total generation capacity — were built: eight wind farms (400 MW), 138 small hydropower plants (90 MW), 53 biogas power plants (54 MW), 107 solar power plants (9 MW), and one biomass power plant (2.4 MW). These incentives also financed 12 high-efficiency cogeneration plants (36 MW) and one waste-to-energy plant in Vinča (30 MW), bringing the total number of built plants to 320. On what Serbia gained, importing the 13.6 TWh would have cost EUR 1.469 billion — about EUR 50 million less than the EUR 1.519 billion paid for feed-in tariffs; Stojadinović stresses that for this difference Serbia gained a renewable-energy market with numerous operating companies and significant employment, since it does not keep statistics on so-called 'green jobs' but estimates that running and maintaining these plants requires between 400 and 650 full-time employees. The construction of the power plants and related works required involving about 3,500 workers. EPS's calculation is also relevant: the company obtained 13.6 TWh for EUR 484 million (3.6 eurocents per kWh), whereas buying that same amount on the market would have cost an estimated EUR 1.469 billion. The regulated electricity price for households at which EPS sold this purchased electricity changed over time, from 5.12 eurocents per kWh in 2013 rising every year to 8.78 eurocents per kWh in 2025. In his final assessment Stojadinović says the feed-in tariff system was both successful and necessary for spurring renewable-energy-sector development; through its implementation Serbia gained a renewable-energy market including power plants, experience, and employment it previously lacked, contributed to fulfilling international obligations — including binding targets for the share of renewables in gross final energy consumption — avoided 8.1 million tonnes of CO2 emissions (whose market value is estimated at around EUR 567 million, calculated at EUR 70 per tonne), and generated electricity without air pollution or other negative impacts caused by coal-fired generation.
items.title: Evaluating Serbia's feed-in tariffs: EUR 1.5 billion paid out over 12 years

items.summary:
World stocks slipped on Wednesday (November 18) as investors digested Nvidia's better-than-expected sales forecast while bracing for Anthropic's market debut, which is seen as a major test of the AI investment boom. MSCI's gauge of global equities fell 0.1 per cent, with European shares losing 0.2 per cent across bourses in Frankfurt, Paris and London; the London decline was dragged down by rising UK inflation. The move nonetheless represented steadiness for European equities after they suffered their biggest one-day drop in eight months on Tuesday. Within Europe, tech stocks rose 1.3 per cent, with chip-equipment heavyweight ASML up 3.6 per cent.

The top item on investors' agenda was AI chip company Nvidia, which had given a better-than-expected sales forecast on Tuesday amid uncertainty about its future leadership; its chairman told investors that the company would not rehire co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO. Wall Street was set for gains, with S&P 500 e-mini futures up 0.4 per cent and Nasdaq 100 E-minis up 0.9 per cent, following a Tuesday selloff in which US stocks had fallen before Nvidia's report.

Fleura Shiyanova, an equity analyst at Kepler Unigestion in Switzerland, said: "Nvidia is an AI bellwether and a lot of people pay attention to what they guide... Anything they decide to change will go through various value chains within the AI theme." In oil markets, Brent crude futures trimmed losses to stand 0.7 per cent lower at $92.70 a barrel following data showing increased US crude and fuel inventories last week, although ongoing Middle East conflict and disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz limited those losses.

Nvidia's results helped Asian shares outside Japan eke out a slim gain of 0.1 per cent to break a four-day losing streak; Japan's Nikkei 225 gained 0.3 per cent after several reversals. The next health check on the AI industry would come as Anthropic prepared to price its shares later Wednesday ahead of an IPO that could value the company at as much as $1.4 trillion, with Bloomberg News reporting the firm had guided its IPO price to the top of its range or above.

Jake Behan, head of capital markets at Direxion in New York, said: "I've looked at this whole week as a referendum on AI... Nvidia gave us a read on the buildout, and Anthropic is about to give us a read on investor appetite for the next generation of AI companies." In currency markets, the US dollar index was up 0.2 per cent at 103.78 after earlier reaching its highest level since President Donald Trump's April 2025 tariff announcement; the euro hit its latest low since April 2025 and fell 0.3 per cent to $1.096, while the yen stood flat against the dollar at 159.30.

Data showed Japan's exports rose for a 14th successive month in October, driven by demand for semiconductor-related shipments. The yield on the US 10-year Treasury bond was down 0.6 basis point at 5.095 per cent; St Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem, a non-voter this year, said the Federal Reserve may need several rate hikes to bring inflation under control and should act soon. British government bond yields fell after softer-than-expected inflation data led investors to scale back bets on a December rate rise.
items.title: Global Stocks Slip as Investors Digest Nvidia Forecast and Await Anthropic IPO

items.summary: Shares of AI-related companies rose on Wednesday after Nvidia posted a stronger-than-expected fourth-quarter revenue forecast, easing investor concerns about demand and the chipmaker's outlook following the departure of longtime CEO Jensen Huang. Nvidia shares climbed 3.5 per cent in premarket trading after it projected Q4 revenue at $130 billion plus or minus 3 per cent, above analysts' consensus estimate of $125.25 billion. The company also ruled out rehiring Huang, whose exit last week over revelations of extramarital affairs ended three decades of founder-led control. Nvidia has been the centerpiece of the AI trade, supplying chips that power most AI data centers and financing infrastructure built around its own hardware; this strategy has driven demand but raised questions about circular funding between the chipmaker and its customers. Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo, noted that strong earnings have given management time while reinforcing confidence in broader infrastructure demand, though the next rally leg may depend on which companies can convert that demand into sustainable profits. Nvidia-backed neocloud firms CoreWeave and Nebius Group jumped 5.4 per cent and 7 per cent respectively, while data center names Applied Digital, IREN, Core Scientific and Hut 8 also rose between 5.3 per cent and 6.6 per cent. Chip stocks broadly gained: Advanced Micro Devices up 2.9 per cent, Broadcom up 2.9 per cent, Intel up 1.8 per cent; Micron Technology up 3.2 per cent; Western Digital and Sandisk up 3.1 per cent and 3.6 per cent respectively. Photonic makers Lumentum and Coherent, along with AI server builders Dell, HPE and Super Micro, gained between 3.2 per cent and 6 per cent each. AI hyperscalers Oracle, Alphabet, Amazon.com, Meta Platforms and Microsoft rose modestly between 0.4 per cent and 2.8 per cent. Some Japanese tech stocks closed higher alongside an upbeat session for South Korean giants Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. The AI trade has faced pressure since Democratic midterm wins stoked fears of tougher regulation on data center buildouts, pushing the Nasdaq into correction territory earlier in the month. The next test comes as Anthropic prepares to price its public offering later Wednesday, which could value the company at up to $1.4 trillion.
items.title: Nvidia's Strong Forecast Lifts AI Stocks Amid Demand Fears

items.summary: Google is positioning its generative AI music capabilities around the idea that the technology will assist artists rather than replace them. Over the past year, Google has rolled out several generative AI music features, including Flow Music — acquired in February when it purchased the startup ProducerAI — which lets users create songs from a single prompt and competes with AI music platforms such as Suno and Udio. Rather than framing its technology purely around generation, Google's pitch to artists is that it can function like an existing creative tool, similar to Auto-Tune or MIDI. To demonstrate this, Google launched Flow Music Sessions earlier this year, an artist residency program for those interested in integrating the technology into their own workflows. Residents work within Spaces, a Flow Music feature inherited from ProducerAI that enables artists to vibe code their own tools and plugins. Some artists remain uneasy about fusing art with artificial intelligence, a concern dating back to ChatGPT's launch in 2022. Google has historically entered the creator economy through other channels; it grew YouTube into a video-sharing platform rivaling cable largely by giving independent creators platforms on their own terms — an approach it is now betting could win over AI-wary artists similarly. Avanti Singh, a sound designer and Flow Music resident quoted in Semafor, said he draws creative fuel from making things himself rather than prompting an entire song to be created, since the most enjoyable parts for him are writing lyrics, singing, and collaborating. Mike Costanzo, a producer in the residency, built a 'perfect kick' plugin in Spaces that reduces the time needed to find a suitable kick drum; he selects a genre, taps a musical key to tune the drum, and lets the plugin handle the rest. Separately, Google has faced criticism over its AI music generation: a group of independent musicians and songwriters filed a lawsuit in March alleging that Google trained its Lyria 3 model on copyrighted YouTube recordings without permission or compensation.
