The article reports that India has imposed an effective import duty of 162.5% on bulk Scotch whisky, triggering a dispute with major liquor companies including Pernod Ricard, Diageo and Bacardi months after the India-UK trade agreement reduced tariffs on Scotch to 75%. The higher duty exceeds the 150% tariff that applied before the pact came into effect.

According to Reuters reporting citing eight sources and a government document, Indian investigators believe liquor companies have been using incorrect customs classifications to import bulk Scotch concentrates used as raw material for manufacturing blended whiskies. Investigators argue these imports should be classified under a newly created category called "compound alcoholic preparations," which attracts a 150% tariff; an additional consumption tax then takes the effective duty to 162.5%, per a government document reviewed by Reuters.

This marks the first major trade-related disagreement following the implementation of the India-UK agreement on July 15, and centers specifically on customs classification of bulk Scotch imports. While liquor companies including Pernod Ricard and Diageo believe both bulk and bottled Scotch should qualify for the reduced 75% tariff under the pact, Indian investigators contend that incorrect classification must stop due to its "substantial revenue implications" for the government.

The dispute has left thousands of litres of bulk Scotch in more than 80 shipping containers belonging to Pernod Ricard, Diageo and Bacardi stuck at Indian ports. Under a provisional release arrangement pending investigation, companies must pay 75% of goods value upfront while covering the remainder through bank guarantees; Pernod Ricard and Diageo have moved to arrange these guarantees and additional funding for business continuity, while Bacardi is still evaluating its next steps.

The arrangement could strain working capital, particularly for smaller manufacturers needing collateral. An Indian liquor industry executive told Reuters that "meeting the production requirements is extremely critical, even though bank guarantees stress working capital." The dispute also affects domestic producers including Mumbai-listed Radico Khaitan, Allied Blenders and Distillers and Tilaknagar Industries.

About 80% of Scotch whisky imports from Britain by volume arrive in bulk, making these shipments important for India's liquor manufacturing. Most are used to produce Indian-Made Foreign Liquor (IMFL) whiskies through blending small quantities of Scotch with other spirits into mass-market products cheaper than fully imported brands such as Chivas Regal and Johnnie Walker.

The higher duty has raised concerns about retail prices; companies had already reduced Scotch product prices after the July pact, but uncertainty over import costs now looms. Any prolonged disruption could affect blended whisky production in India, though the extent of impact on retail prices remains uncertain. Whisky tariffs were among contentious issues during negotiations leading to the agreement.

The UK-based Scotch Whisky Association estimated the pact could boost Scotch exports to India by $1.34 billion over five years, and had described duty reductions as a significant benefit. The British government says it is working with New Delhi to resolve the dispute while India indicated the matter would be settled soon.
items.title: India Imposes 162.5% Duty on Bulk Scotch Despite India-UK Trade Pact Tariff Cuts

items.summary: India and the United States are moving closer to concluding a proposed interim trade agreement, though its formal signing remains delayed pending clarity on Washington's evolving tariff framework and ongoing Section 301 investigations. Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal said on Wednesday (November 18) that negotiations and the legal text of the agreement were in their final stages and would be completed soon, but cautioned that actual signing would take longer because the United States had not yet finalized its new tariff structure. The proposed interim trade agreement was announced in February 2026, when Prime Minister Narendra Modi and US President Donald Trump outlined a framework for expanding bilateral trade. However, the tariff environment has changed since then: the US Supreme Court struck down the legal basis of the earlier reciprocal tariff framework in February, prompting Washington to develop a new tariff architecture. Agrawal noted that the agreement had originally been negotiated against the backdrop of the earlier executive tariff system, making it necessary for India to understand how the new structure would affect its exporters before signing. Two US investigations under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 represent key uncertainties. The first examined whether trading partners were effectively prohibiting imports of goods produced using forced labour; following that investigation, the US imposed an additional 10% tariff on Indian goods in July 2026. India was placed in a lower tariff category compared with several other economies, which faced a 12.5% additional duty under the final measures. The second investigation concerns structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors across major trading partners, including India, China, the European Union, Japan, South Korea and Mexico; it was initiated by the US Trade Representative in March 2026, and its outcome is still awaited and could determine whether additional tariffs are imposed. Agrawal said this uncertainty made it difficult to sign an agreement expected to provide greater certainty to businesses and exporters. Despite the delay, India has indicated negotiations are progressing and that Washington acknowledged New Delhi's demand for a comparative tariff advantage. Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said on November 15 that India and the US had already agreed Indian goods would receive preferential market access with lower duties than those imposed on competing countries, an assurance significant for Indian exporters seeking to retain competitiveness in the American market.
items.title: India-US trade deal nears final stage but signing delayed by tariffs and investigations

items.summary: At the ongoing COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, a proposal for a standalone UNFCCC agenda item on mountains' vulnerability to climate change was ultimately edged out by competing priorities — including a flagship electrification proposal — but its concerns still made it into the summit's draft cover text. The bid had been championed by Nepal, which suffered devastating flash floods from a rock-ice avalanche in August, together with Bhutan and Kyrgyzstan; Nepal argued that mountain vulnerability has long been underrepresented within UNFCCC core decision-making tracks and called for integrating mountain-specific priorities into adaptation, finance and loss-and-damage frameworks. When the standalone item co-proposed with Bhutan was not adopted, Lila Pieters Yahia, Nepal's UN Resident Coordinator, said Nepal pivoted to mainstreaming cryosphere and mountain priorities across existing negotiating tracks — a move she described as yielding concrete results. The draft cover text, released on November 16 and likely to undergo several revisions before finalisation at the summit's conclusion on November 20, recognises the particular vulnerability of mountain regions and glacier-dependent communities and proposes work programmes dedicated to resilience building and scientific understanding of these vulnerabilities. Yahia stressed that a dedicated focus requires consistent solidarity between developed and developing Parties — matching Nepal's leadership with commensurate action, investment and cooperation.
items.title: Nepal and Bhutan's mountain agenda edged out of COP31 as cryosphere losses loom near-certain at 1.5°C
